Pregnancy

Pregnancy and parenting after your baby has died

Updated: November 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A new pregnancy can bring hope alongside grief for the baby who died. You may find appointments reassuring, frightening or both, and those feelings can continue after birth. Support should recognise your earlier baby and the particular circumstances of their death. You do not have to feel constantly positive to deserve good care.

Start with the history, not a blanket risk label

Tell your maternity team early that your previous baby died, including what happened during pregnancy, birth and the neonatal period: the time shortly after birth. A neonatal death is different from a stillbirth, although both can deeply affect a later pregnancy. The cause, where known, and your current health help determine what medical care is useful now.

Ask for a review of the previous records and any investigation results. Depending on the findings, the plan may involve an obstetrician, specialist midwife, genetic counsellor or other clinician. Some services describe pregnancy after loss as high risk to organise extra care; the label does not mean that every family has the same risk or needs the same scan schedule. Continue routine maternity appointments as well.

Make appointments easier to navigate

Ask who will coordinate your care, whether you can see a familiar team and whom to contact between visits or overnight. If a pregnancy-after-loss clinic is available, discuss a referral. If returning to the same hospital feels painful, explain this and ask about realistic alternatives, continuity and transfer of records rather than simply missing appointments.

With your agreement, a note in your maternity record can explain the loss and how you would like staff to refer to your baby. This may reduce repeated retelling. Take a trusted person if helpful, bring written questions and record the answers. You can ask staff to pause, explain a result again or arrange another conversation when there is too much to absorb.

Plan around dates and settings that bring back memories

The previous baby’s birthday, the anniversary of their death, a scan room or a familiar stage of pregnancy may bring a surge of fear. Tell the team which dates and settings matter to you. Agree what support could help, such as a longer conversation, a familiar clinician or a quieter appointment arrangement where available.

Extra scans can sometimes help, but reassurance may be brief and more monitoring can also increase anxiety. Ask what each scan can answer and whether it is clinically indicated. Your preferences can change. A flexible plan should include how to obtain emotional support as well as medical assessment, without promising that either can remove all uncertainty.

Do not let anxiety hide a new physical concern

You can be anxious and have a symptom that needs checking at the same time. Once you know your baby’s usual movement pattern, call maternity care immediately if it changes, slows or stops. Do not wait until morning or for the next booked scan. There is no need to prove that your concern is more than anxiety before asking for assessment.

A home Doppler cannot show that a baby is well, even if you hear a heartbeat. Follow the team’s instructions for other new symptoms, including bleeding, leaking fluid or pain. Keep the maternity contact number somewhere easy to find. A previous reassuring visit does not replace assessment of a new concern.

Use everyday support without turning coping into a test

Some days it may help to plan only the next few hours: a meal, a rest, a short comfortable walk or time with a friend. Writing down worries or keeping a diary can help some people organise feelings; others prefer talking or a quiet activity. Choose manageable things you enjoy, and stop an activity if it increases distress.

Peer support can reduce isolation, especially when others understand pregnancy or parenting after loss. You can decide which conversations or online groups feel useful and take breaks from distressing stories. Partners may grieve differently and need their own support. None of these suggestions requires you to stop missing your baby or replaces professional help when daily life is becoming difficult.

Ask for mental health care when fear takes over

Tell your midwife, doctor or mental health professional if worry is hard to control, you avoid needed care, distressing memories keep returning, or you cannot sleep even when you have the opportunity. Persistent low mood, loss of interest or difficulty functioning also deserves assessment. You do not have to wait until things become unbearable, and grief does not automatically mean you have a psychiatric disorder.

Ask for someone with experience of perinatal loss or trauma. Counselling or psychological therapy may help, and some people benefit from medication after an individual discussion. If you already take prescribed treatment, review it with the prescriber rather than stopping it yourself. Medical checks and mental health support can work together; repeated scans are not a complete treatment plan for severe anxiety.

Prepare a birth plan and a small set of essentials

Discuss the place of birth, who you want with you, communication preferences and any hospital spaces you would prefer to avoid. Ask what support will continue after birth and who will assess the new baby. The timing and method of birth need an individual discussion about the current pregnancy, previous experience and your wishes; an earlier birth is not automatically the safest answer to fear.

You do not have to buy everything or pack alone. A trusted person can help prepare a modest bag and keep supplies until needed. For a journey home by car, arrange a suitable, correctly fitted rear-facing newborn seat beforehand. Have a safe infant sleep space and basic care supplies ready too. Ask the hospital what it can provide; do not assume clothes or nappies will be available. Preparing does not cause a bad outcome.

A new baby does not replace the baby who died

Relief or happiness can coexist with sadness, guilt or fear after the birth. Feeling joy does not erase your earlier baby, and continuing grief does not mean you are ungrateful for the new one. You may want to speak about both children, use the baby’s name or keep memories in a way that feels right to you.

Bonding may feel immediate or may develop gradually. Tell the midwife, health visitor or baby’s clinician if fear makes feeding, holding, resting or accepting help difficult. Arrange follow-up for your own wellbeing as well as the baby’s health. Practical help and sensitive support can matter after discharge, when the intensive contact of pregnancy has ended.

Make nights safer without relying on constant checking

Put your baby on their back for every sleep, on a firm, flat, level infant sleep surface with a fitted sheet and no pillows, loose bedding or soft objects. Share your room, with the baby in their own sleep space, for at least the first six months. Avoid falling asleep with the baby on a sofa or armchair. These practices reduce risk; no arrangement can promise that every illness or loss is preventable.

Consumer breathing or heart-rate monitors are not a proven way to prevent sudden infant death syndrome and cannot replace safe sleep or medical assessment. If a clinician prescribes monitoring for a specific condition, follow that plan. Tell your care team if repeated checking keeps you awake or feels impossible to resist. Ask for help with anxiety and a realistic rest plan, rather than trying to stay awake all night to keep the baby safe.

Know when distress needs urgent help

Unwanted frightening thoughts can happen during pregnancy or after birth. A thought that upsets you is not the same as wanting to act on it. Tell a clinician promptly if thoughts recur, cause strong distress or interfere with caring for yourself or the baby. You deserve an assessment that listens carefully rather than assumes what a thought means.

Thoughts of suicide need urgent professional help. If you intend to harm yourself or the baby, cannot keep either of you safe, or experience hallucinations, unusual fixed beliefs or marked confusion after birth, seek emergency care. Ask a trusted adult to stay and help with the baby while help is arranged. Do not wait for a routine appointment or try to manage a possible psychiatric emergency alone.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Agree how the previous history, current findings and your preferences shape appointments and support.

Write down important dates, a contact between visits and the plan for care after birth.

Use support for grief and anxiety alongside medical care and safe infant-care practices.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help keep questions, appointments and support contacts together. It cannot predict recurrence, replace fetal assessment or monitor a baby’s breathing.

When to seek help

Call maternity care immediately for a change in your baby’s usual movements. Seek prompt professional help when anxiety, distressing thoughts or sleeplessness interfere with daily life. Immediate danger, inability to keep yourself or the baby safe, or possible postpartum psychosis needs emergency care.

Evidence notes updated: November 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Ask for a care plan based on the previous baby’s death and this pregnancy, with named contacts.
  • Tell the team about difficult anniversaries, places and appointments so support can be planned.
  • Report changed fetal movements immediately; worry does not make a physical concern less important.
  • Get help preparing essential travel and sleep arrangements if doing it yourself feels overwhelming.
  • Grief can continue after a new birth. Support should continue too.

Frequently asked questions

Will I need more specialist appointments?

You may benefit from specialist review and additional care, but the plan depends on what happened previously, the current pregnancy and your needs. Ask who leads the plan, which scans are recommended and how to get help between visits. There is no single schedule for every neonatal death.

How can I manage anxiety during this pregnancy?

Tell the maternity team what is hardest, identify difficult milestones and ask about counselling or specialist perinatal mental health support. Extra scans may offer only temporary reassurance. Persistent fear, poor sleep or difficulty coping needs attention alongside obstetric care.

What can help with sadness and grief day to day?

Small routines, rest, writing, a gentle activity or talking with someone who understands may help. Choose what feels manageable and allow mixed feelings. If distress makes daily life difficult, ask for professional support rather than expecting yourself to cope through distraction alone.

What if I keep checking the new baby and cannot sleep?

Speak with your midwife, health visitor or clinician. Follow safe-sleep guidance, arrange practical help and ask for assessment of persistent anxiety or intrusive thoughts. A consumer monitor or staying awake all night is not a substitute for support or a reliable way to prevent a death.

Can I ask to use a different hospital?

Yes, explain why the previous setting is difficult and ask about available options. Discuss the clinical facilities you may need, transfer of records and continuity of care. If a change is not possible, the team may be able to adjust rooms, appointments or support.

What if buying baby things feels too difficult?

Ask someone you trust to help and keep the task small. Essential preparations still matter: a safe sleep space, basic supplies and a suitable car seat if travelling home by car. Ask what help is available rather than postponing every arrangement until after discharge.

Is it wrong to feel happy while still grieving?

No. You can welcome a new baby and continue to love and miss the baby who died. There is no requirement to feel one emotion at a time or to have finished grieving before forming a new relationship.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
